newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK--Debate begins on next rate hike.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK--Debate begins on next rate hike.

text.p: After greeting the first rise in interest rates in more than two years, the bond market will be sharply focused on upcoming economic reports to see if another rate tightening is on its way, analysts said.
On Tuesday, the Federal Reserve raised the federal funds rate by 25 basis points to 5.50 percent from 5.25 percent.
Economists said the Fed's accompanying statement, which explains the reasons behind the rate hike, clearly left the door open to future rate hikes.

"So the question is, where do we go from here," asked Kevin Flanagan, money market economist at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc. "From here on in, we are going to have to continue to scrutinize data to see where the Fed will go in May."

The first piece of data coming after the Fed's decision will be February durable goods, due at 0830 EST/1330 GMT on Wednesday. Economists forecast a drop of 0.4 percent compared to a strong rise of 4.0 percent in January.
Excluding the hefty defense component, durable goods orders are expected to fall 0.6 percent.

"If durable goods are negative as I expect ... that will be slightly positive because any continuation of the strength we have seen would imply another firming (of rates)," said Philip Braverman, chief economist at DKB Securities Corp.
But bonds could suffer ahead of more significant data due next week, including the National Association of Purchasing Management's Index and other indicators.
"We have some room to the downside," said an analyst, who said he does not believe the bond market has priced in another rate rise as yet.
The market also will be closely focused on two government auctions tomorrow. The U.S. Treasury will sell $13.75 billion of one-year bills and $12.5 billion of five-year notes.
Any sign of foreign buying at the auctions could generate healthy enthusiasm in the bond market, an analyst said.
The reception to the rate hike overseas from investors in Tokyo, London and other major international markets could also set the tone for trading, analysts said.

"The question up for discussion now is whether they will tighten again in May or July. Clearly they will go again, but if the numbers are soft in the next three to five months, maybe we can put off a tightening until July," said Mark Pawlawk, a trader at Prudential Securities Inc.
The Federal Reserve added temporary reserves to the U.S. banking system on Tuesday through a round of overnight system repurchase agreements.
Funds are expected to open at 5.63 percent on Wednesday, analysts said.
Late Friday afternoon, three-month bill rates were up one basis point to yield 5.40 percent. Six-month bill rates were up 4/32 at 5.59 percent. Year bill rates were up 6/32, yielding 5.88 percent.
Two-year notes were off 3/32 at 6.31 percent. Five-year notes were off 11/32 yielding 6.65 percent. Ten-year notes were off 13 ticks to yield 6.76 percent.
The long bond suffered even heavier losses, off 17/32, driving the yield up to 6.97 percent.
